title: Designing a FINRA for Frontier AI
gist: A FINRA-style self-regulatory organization for frontier AI has moved from proposal to active White House consideration in three months, with Google, Anthropic, OpenAI, Demis Hassabis and reportedly Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent all converging on the structure. The piece is a detailed design blueprint: a 10^26 FLOP membership threshold, CAISI split out of NIST as supervisor, an independent-majority board insulated by Trump v. Slaughter, a compute-provider assessment for funding, and licensed corporate safety officers — with the explicit warning that the alternative is not deregulation but the episodic, reactive interventions of the past two months.

themes.theme: From ad hoc pressure to a designed regime

insights.claim: A FINRA-style self-regulatory organization for frontier AI went from an April proposal to active executive-branch review within roughly three months, with Anthropic, OpenAI and Google each publishing federal AI governance frameworks in June and Google branding its version a 'FARO'.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Industry-wide convergence on a single regulatory architecture in one quarter is an unusually fast policy cascade — the structure is likely to be the default template Congress works from.
insights.quote: Google adopted the FINRA structure and branded it a “FARO.”
insights.locator: A recent idea for governing frontier artificial intelligence

insights.claim: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent reportedly helped develop a proposal — under review by White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles — for an independent frontier AI regulator modeled on FINRA and reporting to the SEC.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Treasury and SEC involvement means AI oversight may land inside financial-regulatory machinery rather than a purpose-built tech agency.
insights.locator: Days later, Bloomberg reported that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent

insights.claim: When Anthropic released Fable 5 the Commerce Department imposed export controls and forced the company to disable it, then the White House applied similar pressure on OpenAI, with both restrictions later lifted through informal negotiations.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Model releases are already subject to discretionary, unappealable shutdown by the executive — a material and unpriced operating risk for frontier labs.
insights.locator: When Anthropic released Fable 5

insights.claim: Congress could in theory give a direct regulator every SRO advantage — off-schedule pay, industry funding, exemption from notice-and-comment timelines, industry technical committees — but in practice it has never done so, and when it wants a fast expert regulator it reaches for the SRO form.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: The case for the SRO is political feasibility, not theoretical superiority — the design will be judged on what Congress will actually enact.
insights.quote: Congress has never given a direct regulator these features, but it has assembled them repeatedly in SROs.
insights.locator: Limitations and Next Steps

insights.claim: The president could invoke the Defense Production Act to sponsor a voluntary agreement among AI developers forming an antitrust-exempt proto-SRO, which could develop testing guidelines for CAISI approval while the executive conditions federal procurement on compliance.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: A pre-legislative path exists that could bind frontier labs via procurement leverage within months — watch for a DPA voluntary agreement as the leading indicator.
insights.locator: But scaffolding can go up now

themes.theme: The SRO form and membership boundary

insights.claim: A supervised self-regulatory organization is defined by mandatory membership, industry funding, and a supervising agency with authority to direct or veto its actions, with SRO rules binding members with the force of law subject to appeal to the supervisor and then federal court.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: The three-feature test is the checklist for judging whether any proposed AI body has real teeth or is voluntary window dressing.
insights.locator: A supervised self-regulatory organization (SRO), like FINRA

insights.claim: Membership should initially extend to any entity maintaining an AI model trained on 10^26 or more floating point operations, a threshold only a handful of models on the market today clear.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: A concrete compute line drawn just above the current frontier — it captures only the top few labs today but sweeps in every future scaled model.
insights.locator: The threshold should be usable now but designed to change

insights.claim: Because membership determines both who bears compliance costs and who votes on the rules, incumbents have a direct interest in setting the frontier-developer boundary to their own advantage.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: The threshold fight is the real regulatory-capture battleground — watch lobbying on the definition, not on the substantive safety rules.
insights.locator: Because membership determines both who bears compliance costs

themes.theme: Choosing the supervisor after Trump v. Slaughter

insights.claim: Now that the president can remove the leadership of independent agencies at will, formal agency independence is no longer a reason to prefer one supervisor over another, and the choice turns instead on expertise and institutional fit.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Removal-power jurisprudence has quietly reshaped all regulatory design debates — insulation must now be engineered through private boards, not agency status.
insights.locator: The Supervisor

insights.claim: Under the SRO model, regulatory independence comes not from the supervising agency but from the SRO's nonprofit board, which lies beyond presidential removal power.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: The central structural argument for the SRO form in the current legal environment: it is the only remaining way to buy insulation from partisan swings.
insights.locator: Under the SRO model, independence comes not from the supervisor

insights.claim: The SEC has unmatched experience overseeing SROs but lacks the technical expertise and clearance infrastructure to evaluate models for cyber or biological threats, which is the decisive weakness in the reported Bessent plan.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Direct critique of the plan reportedly under White House review — argues the frontrunner agency cannot actually do the testing job.
insights.locator: The Bessent plan reportedly names the SEC

insights.claim: CAISI should be split, with interagency coordination and frontier pre-deployment model evaluation forming the core of a new supervisor housed in Commerce but separated from NIST, while standards development, international coordination and foreign-adversary capability assessment stay inside NIST.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: A concrete reorganization proposal — a CAISI/NIST split would be the observable first move toward a statutory AI supervisor.
insights.locator: CAISI may need to be split

themes.theme: Board composition as the anti-capture mechanism

insights.claim: Only the SRO board should be able to remove its own members, who should hold staggered terms exceeding four years, making the board the most robust available mechanism for insulating frontier AI governance from partisan whiplash after Trump v. Slaughter.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Terms longer than a presidential cycle are the specific design feature that decouples AI rules from the election calendar.
insights.locator: After Trump v. Slaughter

insights.claim: Independent governors should form the board majority and outnumber industry governors by two or three seats, following FINRA's current split of 12 public governors against 10 industry governors.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: A benchmark ratio drawn from a working SRO — deviations from roughly 12:10 in any AI proposal signal capture risk.
insights.locator: The majority of board members should be independent governors

insights.claim: AI governors need judgment, political savvy and adversarial-oversight skills rather than elite technical credentials, a profile closer to an activist investor than an eminent academic, contradicting Hassabis's call for Turing Award winners.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Directly disputes the labs' preferred board profile — technical eminence without adversarial instincts is precisely what makes a captured board.
insights.quote: closer to the profile of an activist investor than an eminent academic
insights.locator: Board-member qualifications should reflect the role

insights.claim: The AI supervisor should combine FERC's power to order a proposal on a specified topic with the SEC's power to abrogate, add to and delete from SRO rules, plus a statutory deadline and the ability to implement its own rule on inadequate response.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Names the exact statutory powers to look for in any AI SRO bill — FERC-style request authority alone is toothless because it carries no consequences.
insights.quote: abrogate, add to, and delete from
insights.locator: Two existing models inform the mechanism

insights.claim: The private nondelegation doctrine prohibits SRO rules from taking effect without government approval, and some courts have indicated it also requires the supervisor to hold power to edit those rules.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Constitutional constraint that caps how much authority any AI SRO can hold — pure industry self-governance is not legally available.
insights.locator: The private nondelegation doctrine prohibits

insights.claim: Enforcement is the least developed component of every supervised AI SRO proposal to date: there is rough consensus that models should meet standards before deployment, but the proposals do not say who checks compliance or what happens when a developer contests or violates a determination.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: The gap in the labs' own frameworks is exactly where their obligations would bite — a sign the published proposals are not yet serious commitments.
insights.locator: Enforcement

insights.claim: AI enforcement would primarily be an examination function, with enforcement staff separate from the technical staff who design tests auditing developer practices across the full model life cycle including data selection, training and post-deployment monitoring.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Continuous auditing rather than one-time certification implies a permanent compliance cost line for every frontier lab.
insights.locator: As in finance, AI enforcement would primarily be an examination function

insights.claim: SRO enforcement is self-sustaining because members want their rivals scrutinized — each developer faces different compliance costs for different rules, so some frontier firm will always benefit from enforcement of any particular standard.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Heterogeneous compliance costs turn competitors into enforcement allies — the mechanism that prevents an industry body from becoming a cartel of mutual forbearance.
insights.locator: The SRO has several incentives to enforce

themes.theme: Staffing, safety-officer licensing and compute-assessment funding

insights.claim: Hiring high-quality AI engineers costs roughly $1 million in annual compensation as a benchmark, which is why the SRO must pay outside government scales and be funded by industry.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: A concrete number showing why any government-salaried AI regulator will be structurally outgunned on talent.
insights.quote: roughly $1 million in annual compensation as a benchmark
insights.locator: Staffing and Budget

insights.claim: Safety officers who sign off on covered evaluations could be required to hold an SRO-issued license, giving them personal accountability and a portable credential, turning the SRO into a professional home for safety personnel comparable to what actuaries and attorneys have.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Personal liability plus a portable credential shifts the incentives of in-house safety staff away from their employer — arguably the single highest-leverage proposal in the piece.
insights.locator: Safety officers who sign off on covered evaluations

insights.claim: The SRO should be funded by an assessment on compute providers who pass the cost through to all consumers, ensuring that foreign and open-weight deployments on U.S. infrastructure also contribute and diluting any single developer's funding leverage.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: A levy at the compute layer is a new cost line for cloud and GPU providers and a way to tax foreign models without regulating them directly.
insights.locator: Funds would come from an assessment on compute providers

insights.claim: Including foreign firms as SRO members is untenable because foreign nationals cannot obtain the security clearances required for sensitive cyber or biological testing essential to SRO examinations.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Clearance requirements structurally exclude foreign labs from AI rulemaking, hardening the split between U.S. and non-U.S. AI governance blocs.
insights.locator: A tempting solution is to include foreign firms as SRO members

insights.claim: Closed-weight foreign models can be regulated by prohibiting cloud hosts, API resellers and deployers from providing access unless the SRO has certified the deployer's U.S. version as compliant.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Puts compliance liability on U.S. cloud and API intermediaries — a direct new regulatory exposure for hyperscalers and model marketplaces.
insights.locator: Regulating closed-weight foreign models is relatively straightforward

insights.claim: Because open-weight developers have no incentive to comply, domestic deployers must bear the cost of compliance and safety testing, with only registry-cleared models deployable and the deployer attesting under penalty that it has not fine-tuned the model to weaken safeguards.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Would impose per-deployment testing cost and personal attestation risk on anyone commercially serving open-weight models in the U.S. — a significant tax on the open-weight ecosystem.
insights.locator: Open-weight foreign models should operate under the same principle

insights.claim: The durable long-run solution identified in Google's white paper is a reciprocity regime in which each country tests its own firms' models and recognizes other countries' deployment approvals.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Mutual recognition of AI safety approvals would be the AI analogue of pharmaceutical or aviation certification treaties — a multi-year, high-value policy destination.
